summary: This RFC defines a P flag in the Prefix Information Option of IPv6 Router Advertisements. It tells clients that the network prefers the deployment model in RFC 9663, where a client uses DHCPv6 prefix delegation, instead of building individual addresses with SLAAC from the on-link prefix.

eli5.summary: A router can put up a sign saying "ask me for your own block of addresses" instead of "just pick one for yourself." The P flag is that sign.

questions: how does a router signal dhcpv6 pd availability
what is the ipv6 ra p flag
does the p flag replace slaac
how does a client react to the p flag
subtitle: A one-bit flag in IPv6 Router Advertisements that tells clients to ask for their own prefix instead of building addresses from the shared one.

tldr.problem: Clients cannot tell whether a network wants them to use DHCPv6 prefix delegation (the model in RFC 9663) or to form individual addresses with SLAAC. Guessing wrong can use up a small network's prefixes or defeat the scalability benefits.
tldr.mechanism: A new P flag in the Prefix Information Option of a Router Advertisement says the network prefers prefix delegation. Clients that support it then ask for a prefix by DHCPv6-PD and treat the Autonomous flag as unset.
tldr.outcome: Networks can roll out the per-client prefix model safely, one prefix at a time. The RFC updates RFC 4861 and RFC 4862 to make room for the flag.

today: RFC 9762 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2025. It is not obsoleted and has no later updates listed. It updates RFC 4861 and RFC 4862.

sections.title: Why a Signal Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 9663 describes an address assignment model where each device gets its own prefix from the network using DHCPv6 prefix delegation (DHCPv6-PD). The device then has plenty of address space for itself, for virtual machines and containers, or for downstream devices. Networks also gain scalability, because infrastructure devices no longer keep per-address state such as the IPv6 neighbor cache.

That model does not suit every network. Many home networks offer prefix delegation but do not hold enough space for every device. The RFC gives an example: if a home network receives a /60 from its ISP and each client takes a /64, the network runs out of prefixes after 15 devices.

So clients need a way to learn which method the network prefers. This document provides it.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school that hands out lockers. A big school can give every kid a whole row, but a tiny school only has a few. Kids need a sign telling them which kind of school this is.

sections.title: Why the Flag Lives in the Router Advertisement
sections.content:
The RFC puts the signal in the Prefix Information Option (PIO) of a Router Advertisement (RA) for two reasons.

  • The client must know before it decides to form addresses with SLAAC. If it forms SLAAC addresses first and later gets a delegated prefix, it either keeps both, which reduces the scalability benefit, or removes the SLAAC addresses, which disrupts applications using them.
  • The preference belongs to one particular prefix. A network might want global addresses from a delegated prefix but a Unique Local Address from another PIO using SLAAC. In multihoming, one upstream may delegate prefixes while another uses PIOs.

Setting the flag expresses a preference, not a command. The delegated prefix a client receives is necessarily different from the one in the PIO.
sections.eli5: The sign has to be on the door before you walk in and grab a seat. And each door can have its own sign, because different rooms can have different rules.

sections.title: The P Flag in the Prefix Information Option
sections.content:
The P flag, also called the DHCPv6-PD Preferred Flag, is a 1-bit flag in the PIO, placed right after the R flag. A PIO with the P flag set means the network prefers prefix delegation over individual addresses from SLAAC or DHCPv6 address assignment. This implies the network has a DHCPv6 server able to delegate prefixes to every device, as RFC 9663 describes.

The flag is independent of the M and O flags in the RA. A network that also wants to serve devices without P flag support SHOULD set M or O to 1 as well, because some devices, such as Customer Edge routers, might not start prefix delegation when both bits are zero.
sections.eli5: The sign is just one tiny switch, up or down, tucked in next to some other switches that were already there.

sections.title: Router and Client Behavior
sections.content:
Routers SHOULD set the P flag to zero by default unless the administrator configures it, SHOULD let the operator set it per advertised prefix, and MUST allow it to be configured separately from the A flag. Changing the P flag MUST NOT automatically change the A flag.

Clients that do not support DHCPv6-PD MUST ignore the P flag. A supporting client keeps, for each interface, a list of every prefix received in a PIO with the P flag set and a non-zero preferred lifetime. A prefix leaves the list when its preferred lifetime reaches zero.

  • When the list grows to one entry, the client SHOULD start requesting prefixes via DHCPv6-PD.
  • When it shrinks to zero, the client SHOULD stop requesting or renewing, if it has no other reason to. Prefixes it already holds keep their lifetimes.
  • If the client already has delegated prefixes and the list changes, it MUST treat that as a configuration change and perform a REBIND, unless the list is now empty.

The client MUST use the prefix length hint to ask for a prefix short enough for SLAAC. While it requests a prefix, it SHOULD NOT use SLAAC on PIOs with both P and A set. If all PIOs have P set, it SHOULD NOT ask for individual addresses (no IA_NA options in Solicit messages). If it gets no suitable prefix, it MAY stop processing the P flag on that interface and fall back to SLAAC or DHCPv6 addresses.

A delegated prefix that is too long for SLAAC MUST be ignored. A shorter one SHOULD be accepted and may be used for the client's own addresses, for VMs or containers, or advertised on another interface, but never back on the interface it came from. The client MUST NOT send or forward packets for the delegated prefix to that interface, to avoid a routing loop. A high-metric discard route is one way to prevent it.

The P flag is only a positive signal. A PIO without it does not mean DHCPv6-PD is absent, and nodes already running prefix delegation, such as CE routers, MUST NOT stop because of it.
sections.eli5: When the sign goes up, a kid who understands it goes to the office and asks for their own row of lockers. When the sign comes down, they can stop asking, but they keep the lockers they already have.

sections.title: Living on a Network with Per-Client Prefixes
sections.content:
When every client has a unique prefix, other clients' addresses are off-link, so traffic first goes to the default router. The router may answer with an ICMPv6 redirect so traffic can flow directly between devices. Hosts supporting the P flag SHOULD therefore process redirects unless configured otherwise. Without redirects, communication between clients on the same link may see higher latency.

For source address selection, a host that creates addresses from a delegated prefix SHOULD treat them as if assigned to the interface on which the prefix was received. In multi-prefix multihoming, a host that supports Rule 5.5 of RFC 6724 SHOULD associate each prefix with the link-local address of the DHCPv6 server or relay that sent the REPLY, and with all such addresses if several distinct ones carried the same prefix.
sections.eli5: If two kids with different locker rows want to swap notes, the note first goes to the office, and the office may say "you can pass these directly." Kids should listen to that advice.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 4861 and RFC 4862
sections.content:
This document updates two older RFCs. In RFC 4861, the note that no DHCPv6 information is available when neither M nor O is set becomes: if the M, O or P flags are not set, no information is available via DHCPv6.

In RFC 4862, Section 5.5.3, the PIO processing steps gain a new step. If the P flag is set and the node implements this RFC, it SHOULD treat the Autonomous flag as unset and use prefix delegation to obtain addresses. The old step about an unset Autonomous flag follows it, and the remaining steps are reordered.
sections.eli5: The old rule book gets two small edits so that it knows about the new sign.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The mechanism shares the security model of SLAAC. Without RA-Guard, an attacker could send RAs with the network's PIO and the P flag set, forcing hosts to ignore the A flag. With no DHCPv6-PD infrastructure, hosts would get no addresses or be delayed while falling back. Without DHCPv6-Shield, an attacker could also run a rogue DHCPv6 server. Toggling the flag could make clients oscillate and issue REBIND requests, though RFC 8415 requires DHCPv6-PD clients to rate-limit their messages. If rogue RAs are allowed, an attacker could disrupt connectivity anyway, so nothing fundamentally new is introduced.

Privacy impact resembles DHCPv6 address assignment: if the same client always gets the same prefix, an observer might identify it by the highest 64 bits of its address. Starting DHCPv6 may reveal minor extra information such as the hostname. Supporting the flag on the sender side raises no privacy concerns.
sections.eli5: A trickster could put up a fake sign to confuse everyone, but a trickster who can already post fake signs could cause trouble anyway.
